groups.context:
No language is built entirely from its own materials. When speakers of different languages trade, travel, or live side by side, words pass from one language to another. Linguists call these words loanwords, although the term is slightly misleading, since a borrowed word is never given back.

Borrowing usually happens when a language lacks a name for something new. English speakers who first encountered foods such as sushi and yogurt simply adopted the Japanese and Turkish names along with the products. Borrowed words rarely stay unchanged, however. Their pronunciation is adjusted to fit the sound system of the new language, and their form may be shortened. In Japanese, for example, the English word "television" became terebi.

Not all borrowing fills a gap. After the Norman Conquest of 1066, French was the language of England's rulers, and thousands of French words entered English even where native words already existed. This is why the animals in the field are called cow and sheep, both Old English words, while the meat on the table is beef and mutton, both from French. Borrowing, in other words, reflects prestige as well as need, and a language's vocabulary is a record of the peoples its speakers have met.

Astronomers long suspected that the Sun was not the only star with planets, but proof was slow to come. A planet shines only by reflected light, and that faint glow is drowned out by the star it circles. Seeing one directly is like trying to spot a firefly beside a lighthouse from many kilometers away. The first planet orbiting a Sun-like star was not confirmed until 1995.

Because direct observation is so difficult, most discoveries have relied on indirect evidence. One approach watches for a wobble: as a planet orbits, its gravity tugs the star slightly back and forth, and this motion subtly shifts the color of the star's light. Another, the transit method, monitors a star's brightness. If a planet happens to pass between the star and Earth, the light dims by a tiny fraction at regular intervals. Space telescopes using this technique have identified thousands of planets.

Neither method is neutral, however. A large planet close to its star produces a stronger wobble and deeper, more frequent dips in brightness than a small, distant one, so giant planets in tight orbits dominated the early lists. Astronomers therefore caution that the catalog reflects the limits of their instruments as much as the true population of planets. Worlds resembling Earth may be common; they are simply harder to detect.

listening.script: Imagine you have a headache, and I give you a pill. Half an hour later, the pain is gone. Now, what if I told you that pill was made of sugar? Nothing in it at all. Would you believe me? Well, this happens all the time, and psychologists call it the placebo effect. A placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient. What does the work isn't the pill. It's your expectation that you're going to feel better. And here's the part I find fascinating. The details of the treatment matter. In experiments, people report more relief from two sugar pills than from one. A placebo they're told is expensive works better than one they think is cheap. So it's really the meaning we attach to the treatment that counts. Is it all imagination, then? Not exactly. When people expect pain relief, their brains actually release natural painkilling chemicals. So the change is real. But let's be careful here. Placebos mostly affect things we feel, like pain or tiredness. A sugar pill won't mend a broken bone. And this is exactly why researchers testing a new medicine give one group the real drug and another group a placebo. Only if the drug beats the placebo can they say it really works.

options: How animals survive in the Sahara

questions.explanation: The professor's puzzle is hot afternoons and cold nights in the Sahara: 'So where does all that heat go?'

listening.script: OK, let's start with a little puzzle. In the Sahara, an afternoon can easily reach forty degrees Celsius. But stay there after dark, and the temperature may fall by twenty degrees or more. On a winter night, it can even come close to freezing. So where does all that heat go? Any ideas? Well, the short answer is: straight up. Let me explain. During the day, the ground soaks up energy from the sun. At night, it gives that energy back as heat, which escapes upward. Now, in most places, something keeps a lot of that heat from getting away. Water. Water vapor in the air and clouds overhead absorb the heat and send part of it back down. They work like a blanket. That's why a cloudy night usually feels milder than a clear one. But desert air is extremely dry, and the sky is almost always clear. There's no blanket. So the heat just leaks away into space. And there's a second reason. Sand itself. Sand warms up fast, but only the top layer gets hot, so it doesn't hold much heat, and it loses it quickly once the sun goes down. Compare that with a tropical rainforest. The air there is full of moisture, so the nights are only a little cooler than the days. Same sun, very different nights.

answers: They return some heat toward the ground.

listening.script: Picture a pasture that belongs to no one and is open to every herder in the village. Each herder asks a perfectly reasonable question: should I add one more cow? Well, the profit from that cow is mine alone. The damage it does to the grass, on the other hand, is shared by everybody. So I add the cow. And so does my neighbor, and hers. Before long, the pasture is bare, and everyone is worse off. In nineteen sixty-eight, the ecologist Garrett Hardin called this the tragedy of the commons, and you can see why the label stuck. Swap the pasture for the open ocean, and the cows for fishing boats, and you have a fair description of overfishing. Notice that nobody in the story is a villain. Each person acts sensibly, and together they wreck the thing they depend on. Hardin saw essentially two ways out: divide the resource into private property, or have the government regulate it. Now, that's where I think he was too gloomy. The political scientist Elinor Ostrom spent decades studying real communities, Swiss mountain villages sharing pastures, farmers sharing irrigation water, and she found that many had managed common resources for centuries. They made their own rules, kept an eye on one another, and punished cheats. So the tragedy is a real risk. It just isn't destiny.

And yet, if you switch off your submarine's lights, the water around you flickers and sparkles. That's bioluminescence, light made by living things, and down there it's not the exception. What's more interesting is what the light is for. The anglerfish dangles a glowing lure in front of its mouth, and you can guess how that ends for a curious little fish. Some shrimp do the opposite. Then there's my favorite trick, and for this one we go a little higher, where a faint glow still filters down from the surface. The hatchetfish has lights along its belly. Odd place for them, isn't it? But seen from below, a fish is a dark shape against that glow. By lighting its belly to match, the hatchetfish erases its own shadow. It hides by shining. Most of this light is blue, because blue travels farthest through seawater. A few dragonfish, though, make red light, which most of their neighbors can't see at all. Dear Professor Haddad,

I hope you are well. I am writing to ask whether you would be willing to write a recommendation letter for me.

groups.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
groups.instructions: Your professor is teaching a class on environmental studies. Write a post responding to the professor's question.

professor.name: Dr. Marchetti
professor.post: This week we are looking at policies designed to reduce plastic waste. Many governments have targeted single-use plastic bags, but they have chosen different tools. Some, such as Kenya and Rwanda, have banned the bags completely. Others, such as Ireland, require stores to charge customers a small fee for each bag. Both approaches aim to change shoppers' habits. Which do you think is the better policy: banning single-use plastic bags or charging a fee for them? Why?

students.name: Yusuf
students.post: I think a ban is better because it is simple and it works immediately. When a fee is small, many shoppers just pay it and keep using plastic bags, especially people with higher incomes. A ban treats everyone the same way. After a few weeks, bringing a reusable bag becomes a normal habit, just like bringing a wallet.

students.name: Greta
students.post: I prefer a fee. A ban removes people's choice, and sometimes a plastic bag is really necessary, for example when you buy fresh fish or forget your own bag. A fee still makes people think twice, and the money collected can pay for recycling programs or beach cleanups. A ban produces no money at all for the environment.

questions.prompt: Express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
questions.explanation:
Model response:

I believe that charging a fee is the better policy, as long as the fee is high enough to matter. Yusuf is right that a very small charge is easy to ignore, but that is an argument for raising the price, not for a ban. Greta mentions that the money can support recycling, and I would add another advantage: a fee is much easier to enforce. When bags are banned completely, some shops keep handing them out secretly, and inspectors must visit every market to stop them. With a fee, stores simply record each bag at the cash register, so the rule is followed almost automatically. Finally, a fee can be adjusted. If people are still using too many bags after a year, the government can increase the charge step by step until the habit really changes.

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 1 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: A trip I remember very well is a visit to my grandparents' village two summers ago. I went with my cousin, and we traveled by train for almost nine hours. The village is in the mountains, so the air was cool and clean, which was a big change from the city. What made the trip memorable was how simple each day was. We helped my grandfather pick apples in the morning, swam in the river in the afternoon, and listened to his stories at night. There was almost no phone signal, so nobody looked at a screen. I came home feeling completely rested.

listening.script: Thank you for taking part in this study. Let's start with your own experience. Please tell me about a trip you took that you remember well. Where did you go, and what made it memorable?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 2 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I am definitely a planner, although I leave a little free time. Before a trip, I book my transportation and my accommodation, and I make a short list of places I really want to see. The main reason is money. Tickets and rooms are usually cheaper when you reserve them early, and as a student I have to be careful with my budget. Planning also saves time, because I don't spend half a morning deciding where to go. However, I never fill the whole schedule. I always keep one afternoon open, since the best moments often happen when you simply walk around without a plan.

listening.script: Some people like to plan every detail of a vacation in advance, while others prefer to decide what to do after they arrive. Which kind of traveler are you, and why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 3 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: I mostly agree. Books and videos can give you facts, but they are chosen and edited by someone else, so you only see what that person wants to show. When you travel, you notice small things that nobody films, such as how people wait in line, how loudly they speak, or what they eat for breakfast. You also have to solve real problems, like buying a ticket in another language, and that teaches you a lot. On the other hand, a short trip can give a false picture, because tourists usually see only the most famous places. So I think travel teaches more, but only if you stay long enough and talk to local people.

listening.script: Now I'd like to ask for your opinion. Some people say that you learn more by traveling to another country than by reading or watching videos about it. Do you agree or disagree? Why?

stages.title: Speaking · Interview question 4 of 4
stages.instructions: Answer the interviewer's question after the beep. You have 45 seconds.

questions.explanation: Model answer: Yes, I think cities should be able to limit tourist numbers when it is really necessary. In very popular places, residents face higher rents, crowded buses, and noise late at night, and some of them finally move away. If that continues, the city loses the local life that made it attractive in the first place. However, I would not close the city to visitors. A better method is to control the busiest places and times, for example by selling a fixed number of tickets for a famous square or museum each day. Cities can also encourage people to come in the quiet season. In this way, tourism still supports local jobs without making life unpleasant for residents.

listening.script: Here is my final question. Popular tourist destinations sometimes become so crowded that daily life gets harder for the people who live there. Do you think cities should limit the number of tourists who can visit? Why or why not?
